extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media researchers, and journalism policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for journalists producing independent email newsletters (on Substack), focusing on career uses, content production practices, monetization, platform effects, and professional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold journalistic norms (objectivity, fairness, balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek to continue to uphold journalistic norms of objectivity, fairness, and balance even when embracing the freedom of work on digital platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees describe using methods of reporting to neutralize personal preconceptions and emphasize fairness (e.g., 'the objectivity of a journalist involves not coming into a story as a blank slate, but in the method that they report the story'). They express concern that without institutional gatekeeping and editing, newsletters may weaken standards of accuracy and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish original reporting from commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that newsletters are 'great for comment' and personal perspective but are often not substitutes for the rigorous reporting required to 'establish the facts in the first place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: treating a newsletter as a substitute for resource-intensive investigative reporting. Guidance: use newsletters for commentary, analysis, or 'writing off the news,' but not as a full replacement for reporting that requires institutional resources and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build an expert persona / niche specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a persona as an expert on a niche topic to publicize work, practice skills, and build a loyal audience (e.g., 'create a persona as an expert on a niche topic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the newsletter to house a body of work that demonstrates expertise (useful for job searches or book proposals), focus on niche topics to leverage 'niche economics' and attract a passionate base rather than a vast user base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization via paid subscriptions (economics & revenue share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use paid subscriptions as a funding stream; note Substack typically takes ~10% of paid subscription fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes examples of subscription pricing ($5–$50/month), revenue potential for top writers (top ten reportedly earn millions), and explicit financial calculations showing many writers cannot reach livable wages without thousands of paid subscribers. Consider tradeoffs when paywalling content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience growth & need for pre-existing following
rubrics_metrics.description: Amassing subscribers is difficult without a pre-established reputation, large digital following, or institutional ties; growth often relies on virality (e.g., Twitter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: starting a newsletter without an existing audience and expecting organic growth. Practical note: many successful Substack writers 'already had these huge Twitter followings.' Reliance on virality makes growth unpredictable and precarious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting frequency and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a posting cadence to keep a newsletter active: active newsletters post frequently (median posting days differ between category-listed and general search results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computational findings: newsletters sorted by category post more often (median 3 days ago) vs. general search (median 58 days). Inactive newsletters have fewer posts (median 7) compared with active ones (median 42). Consistency supports discoverability and audience retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperlinking and citation patterns (ties to established media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsletters commonly link to major media and platform domains (e.g., YouTube, Twitter, New York Times), demonstrating reliance on institutional news and established platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 77% linked to YouTube; only small overlap linking to other newsletters; unique URL appears in only ~2% of newsletters. This indicates siloing and dependence on established outlets for sourcing and visibility rather than creating a self-contained alternative media ecosystem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance personalization with professional norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a personal voice ('keeping that personal note is really important') while integrating journalistic standards and differentiating newsletter content from formal career work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: writers are more open in Substack than in traditional outlets; some separate personal, 'janky' newsletters from their formal reportage. Guidance: preserve dialogic relationships and authenticity but be mindful of methods, fairness, and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform responsibility and content moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the platform's role in moderation, accountability, and support (e.g., Substack's stance as 'platform' vs 'publisher' and its controversy over moderation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees call for more responsibility from Substack for content promoted on the platform; note that Substack has added features like legal advice and writer office hours in response to criticism. Consider platform policies when evaluating risks and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability & financial feasibility of newsletter careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether newsletter writing alone can provide a livable wage; many find it economically unsustainable without substantial subscriber bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: after Substack's cut, earning $2,250/month from 500 subscribers paying $5 is unlikely to be livable; producing multiple posts reduces per-article compensation. Lifeboat users often report disappointment and financial precarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence versus institutional ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that while newsletters can offer independence, many writers remain reliant on institutional outlets for visibility, legitimacy, and sourcing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report emphasizes that newsletters often complement institutional careers (career resource), despite claims of being an alternative model. Use newsletters to augment institutional ties or to leverage them for audience growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience accountability vs advertiser-driven incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscriber-supported models align incentives toward readers rather than advertisers, potentially reducing clickbait and sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees argue that asking readers for support makes writers accountable to their audience's interests and quality, contrasting with ad-driven incentives that favor virality and sensational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial rigor and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the value of rigorous editing and resource-intensive reporting provided by traditional outlets, which may be missing in personal newsletters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns: lack of institutional editing can lead to accuracy issues. Guidance: when possible, incorporate editorial practices or collaborations to preserve standards; use newsletters for commentary while recognizing limits for in-depth reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform design favors writing-centric output and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Substack's features that prioritize textual work and give creators control over subscriber lists, archives, and intellectual property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substack focuses on writing as main output and is designed for writers, which lowers technical barriers compared with more multimedia platforms. Leverage platform tools for distribution and ownership, but be aware of platform business model and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage niche economics and small passionate audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Target specialized topics where a relatively small but passionate subscriber base can sustain a newsletter enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes that because starting costs are low, 'you don’t necessarily need to have a vast user base'—a focused niche can be monetizable if content resonates strongly with a specific audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use newsletter as portfolio and career development tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the newsletter to showcase work, demonstrate ability in a specialization, attract job opportunities, or build a book proposal portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: writers used newsletters to compile a body of work for prospective employers or to demonstrate interest/expertise. Guidance: curate About pages and early posts to clearly communicate purpose and quality to prospective employers or collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize lifeboat function and associated risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that some use newsletters as a lifeboat when other career opportunities are lacking; this role often comes with skepticism about long-term viability and professional identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees in this group describe financial difficulty, burnout, and distance from journalistic identity; they tend to be critical of Substack's feasibility and concerned about the platform supporting existing power structures rather than democratizing media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incentives toward virality and outrage-driven content
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary that subscription dynamics and attention economies can privilege sensationalist or enraging content that drives subscriptions but may degrade quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'stoke rage' or produce outrage for subscriptions. Some writers resist this by prioritizing contextualized analysis, reporting, and conversations beyond echo chambers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for discoverability: taxonomy and category placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use platform discovery features and categories to increase visibility; Substack's taxonomy affects which newsletters are active and discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computational findings show category-listed newsletters are more active and posted more frequently; selecting appropriate categories and maintaining activity help visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build direct audience relationships and community
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate dialogic relationships with readers to build loyalty and reduce hierarchical divides between writer and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsletters can promote closer engagement and openness than traditional publication formats; using personalization and conversational tone can strengthen readership and retention while balancing professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose topics aligned with resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Select topics that are feasible to cover independently (e.g., technology often requires fewer resources than field reporting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consideration: reporting-heavy beats require resources and time; many independent writers gravitate to technology and commentary beats because they are more accessible as solo endeavors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for platform algorithms and Big Tech influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how algorithmic visibility and the broader actions of Big Tech shape what content gains attention and how independent media is discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns include alternative media being 'locked out' or buried in search; writers should be aware of platform dependencies and consider diversification of distribution channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh paywall tradeoffs: accessibility vs growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the tension between paywalling content for revenue and leaving content public to enable virality and subscriber acquisition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paywalls can hide content that might attract new readers; some writers adopt hybrid strategies (free content plus paid extras) and weigh immediate income against long-term growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize concentration of editing resources and status
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that high-quality editing, access, and living wages may remain concentrated in a few established outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: newsletters may function as auditions rather than stable career homes; consider collaborations, networks, or collective models to access editorial support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and respond to attention/metrics incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conscious that digitization emphasizes audience engagement, circulation metrics, and digital attention as measures of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics can drive content strategies; use them thoughtfully rather than letting raw engagement metrics solely dictate editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop personal branding and microcelebrity skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine journalistic networks with entrepreneurship, microcelebrity, and influencer tactics to grow an audience and career opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skills such as regular output, social media promotion, and community engagement are important; interviewees cite advice to 'build your quote-unquote personal brand' and the reality that this is part of the contemporary media career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the newsletter to practice and experiment with writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat newsletters as spaces for professional development, creative projects, and maintaining a writing schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewees describe newsletters as 'passion projects' and places to 'practice the craft,' providing structure and opportunities to write beyond day-job constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of audience composition and partisan dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how media ecosystems and newsletters relate to partisan identities and audience segmentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study's sampling notes partisan range but not representativeness; writers should be mindful that segmentation can limit shared public understanding and contribute to informational silos.
